pages.summary: Box plots: each group's median and quartiles as a box, whiskers to the most extreme values within reach, and outliers beyond.
body: The box spans the lower to the upper quartile with a line at the median; the whiskers reach the farthest values within 1.5 times the box's height of it, and values beyond are drawn alone as outliers. `boxplot` takes the columns of a matrix, or values and a grouping variable, with notches (an interval for the median: boxes whose notches do not overlap differ at about the 5% level), labels, and horizontal boxes. `boxchart` makes the same chart as an object, its groups numbers or categories, coloured by a second grouping when asked.

examples.title: Three samples, one skewed
examples.code:
rng default
X = [randn(60, 1), 1 + 0.5*randn(60, 1), exprnd(1, 60, 1)];
subplot(1, 2, 1), boxplot(X, 'Notch', 'on', 'Labels', {'normal', 'narrow', 'skewed'})
subplot(1, 2, 2), boxchart(categorical(repelem({'a'; 'b'}, 30)), [randn(30, 1); 2 + randn(30, 1)])

pages.summary: Scatter plots by group, and matrices of scatter plots.
body: `gscatter` draws each group of points in its own colour and marker, named in a legend. `plotmatrix` draws every column of a matrix against every other, with histograms on the diagonal; `gplotmatrix` does so by group, the diagonal showing each group's histogram outline. Both give the axes, and a big invisible axes over the whole for a title.

examples.title: Two kinds of points
Three variables at once

pages.summary: A scatter plot with the histograms of x and y beside it, and many points as coloured bins.
body: `scatterhist` draws the points and, below and to the left, the histograms of x and of y (by group if asked, with kernel densities if asked). `scatterhistogram` makes the same chart as an object, from vectors or a table. `binscatter` counts the points in a grid of bins and colours each bin by its count: the shape of a cloud too dense to draw point by point.

examples.title: A correlated pair
Ten thousand points

pages.summary: How a sample is distributed: a histogram with a fitted density, probability and quantile plots, and the empirical distribution function.
body: `histfit` draws a histogram with a density fitted to the data (normal unless another is named) scaled to the counts. `normplot` plots the sorted data against normal quantiles on an axis marked in probabilities: normal data lie near the line through the quartiles. `qqplot` plots a sample's quantiles against the standard normal's, a distribution's or another sample's: points near the line mean the two differ at most in location and scale. `cdfplot` draws the empirical distribution function as steps.

examples.title: A normal sample and a skewed one
examples.code:
rng default
x = 3 + 2*randn(200, 1);
y = exprnd(2, 200, 1);
subplot(2, 2, 1), histfit(x)
subplot(2, 2, 2), histfit(y, 20, 'exponential')
subplot(2, 2, 3), normplot([x, y])
subplot(2, 2, 4), qqplot(x, y)

examples.title: The empirical distribution function

pages.summary: Lines and curves for reference across a plot: least-squares lines, y = m*x + b, and a polynomial.
body: `lsline` fits a straight line to each set of points in the axes (markers without lines) and draws it across their x values, in their colour. `refline` draws y = m*x + b across the axes (with no inputs, the least-squares lines). `refcurve` draws a polynomial, its coefficients from the highest power down.

examples.title: Points, their fit, and two references

pages.summary: Parallel coordinates: each row of data a line across its variables.
body: Each variable has an axis of its own, scaled to its range (or by z-scores, or not at all), side by side; each row is a line joining its values. Groups are coloured apart, which shows which variables separate them. It takes a matrix or a table, and gives a chart object.
